scenario: AITA for not staying home and taking care of my sick wife all weekend? | On Thursday evening my wife started feeling unwell. I encouraged her to go to bed and told her I could handle the kids evening stuff by myself (3 kids, ages 9, 11, and 13). I checked on her after the kids were in bed at 9 and she was fevered- I asked if she wanted any medicine, made sure she had some water, and rubbed her back for a few minutes. I slept in the spare room but got up twice to check on her. The next morning I got the kids ready and off to school, went to a meeting and came home at 10 to take her to the doctor. I worked from home until our cleaning lady came around 1 and asked her to keep an eye on my wife and went back into the office for a couple meetings, picked up the kids and was home around 4. Her fever broke shortly after I got home at 4 and I helped her shower. Our oldest had a school dance and I got some movies and set the youngest 2 up in the den for the evening with pizza and some games so they'd be quiet. I checked on my wife periodically and after the oldest got home me and the 3 kids camped out in the den. On Saturday morning, the kids were restless so I took them out for the day bc I didn't want them to be around the house being loud. I checked on my wife and she was sleeping- I refilled her water and left her a note. Throughout the day I called and sent her messages and my mom took her over some homemade soup and checked on her. We were gone the majority of the day but the kids came home worn out and we crashed in the den again. I checked on my wife as soon as we got home and she was looking better. Sunday morning, the kids and I woke up early, did some yardwork then went to the store to do the weekly grocery shopping. When we got home my wife was up and about and still weak but feeling better. However, she was being really short with me and was in a bad mood. I thought it was just bc she didn't feel well but after a few hours of her making snide comments I asked her if something was wrong and she exploded on me that her family abandoned her while she was sick. She went off about how she always takes care of us when we're sick but we avoided her like the plague and didn't stay home and I made the cleaning lady and my mom take care of her instead of doing it myself. I tried to explain that I didn't want to expose the kids to being sick and I didn't want them around the house being loud while she was trying to rest and I checked on her multiple times. She said I should've sent the kids to my parents or something and stayed home and she can't believe I didn't sleep with her for 3 days. I starting getting angry and told her that I did what I thought was best and she sounded ungrateful bc it wasn't exactly what she would've done. She then called me an asshole. We went to bed angry and didn't really speak this morning. I keep stewing over this bc I don't think that I'm an asshole but maybe I am?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Based on the details you shared, here’s a balanced breakdown of the **pros and cons** of your actions, along with why your wife might feel abandoned—even if your intentions were good. --- ### **Was It Right? (Arguments for Your Approach)** 1. **Protecting the Kids from Illness** - You had a valid concern about exposing your children to your wife’s illness, especially since they were still at school and could spread germs. Keeping them away from her (and vice versa) was a **practical and responsible** move. - Kids can be loud and restless, which might have stressed your wife further. Giving her space to rest was considerate. 2. **Balancing Work and Care** - You took her to the doctor, managed the kids, and worked from home when possible. This shows you were **actively involved** in her care, even if not 24/7. - Your wife might have expected you to **drop everything** (including work and childcare), but you did what you thought was a **realistic compromise**. 3. **Physical Presence ≠ Emotional Presence** - You **did check on her multiple times** (even if not sleeping beside her). Some people feel more supported by **frequent, brief interactions** than constant physical presence. - Your wife might have wanted **more emotional reassurance** (e.g., sitting with her, talking, or just being nearby) rather than practical tasks. 4. **Cultural/Generational Differences** - If your wife grew up in a household where **immediate, hands-on care** (like sleeping in the same room) was the norm, she might have expected the same from you. - Some partners feel **abandoned** when their spouse prioritizes work or the kids over them, even if they’re doing other things. --- ### **Was It Wrong? (Arguments for Your Wife’s Perspective)** 1. **The "Abandoned" Feeling** - Your wife likely felt **emotionally neglected**, not just physically. Even if you were "there" in a logistical sense, she might have wanted **more affection, attention, and companionship** during her illness. - **Sleeping in the spare room for 3 days** (even with check-ins) can feel like **emotional distance**, especially when she’s vulnerable. - Her frustration wasn’t just about **who did the tasks**—it was about **feeling valued and prioritized**. 2. **The Cleaning Lady/Mom "Replacing" You** - She may have resented that **outsiders** (even well-meaning ones) were taking over her care while you were elsewhere. This could feel like **you weren’t fully committed** to her recovery. - If she’s used to being the **primary caregiver** in the family, she might have expected you to **step up as the primary care-giver** to her. 3. **The "I Did What I Thought Was Best" Defense** - Your wife’s anger wasn’t just about **what you did**—it was about **how you communicated it**. She might have felt **unheard** when you didn’t ask her how she wanted to be cared for. - Saying, *"This isn’t what she would’ve done"* (implying her expectations were unreasonable) **escalated the conflict** rather than validating her feelings. 4. **The "Asshole" Label** - Calling her an "asshole" (even in anger) was a **major relationship red flag**. In a vulnerable moment, she needed **compassion, not criticism**, even if you felt justified. - Her reaction was **overwhelming**, but your response **fueled the fire** instead of de-escalating. --- ### **Why This Situation Is So Tricky** - **Different Love Languages**: You might show love through **actions** (checking on her, managing the kids, working to support the family), while she might need **time and presence** (sitting with her, talking, holding her hand). - **Guilt vs. Resentment**: She may feel **guilty for being upset** while sick, but that doesn’t mean her feelings are invalid. **Resentment builds when people feel unappreciated**, even in small ways. - **The "Hero" Trap**: Many partners feel like they **have to be the perfect caregiver** to avoid being seen as selfish. But **perfection isn’t the goal—connection is**. --- ### **How to Repair This** 1. **Acknowledge Her Feelings (Without Defending Yourself)** - Instead of saying *"I did what was best,"* try: > *"I hear how much it hurt you to feel abandoned. I didn’t realize you wanted me to be with you more, even if it was just sitting quietly. I’m sorry I didn’t check in with you about what you needed."* - This **validates her emotions** without making you the "bad guy." 2. **Apologize for the "Asshole" Comment** - Say something like: > *"I’m sorry I called you that. When you’re upset, I should’ve listened more and talked less. I love you, and I want you to know I’m here for you."* - **Apologies without excuses** go further than justifications. 3. **Clarify Your Intentions (Without Blaming Her)** - Explain your perspective **without making her wrong**: > *"I was trying to protect the kids from getting sick and give you space to rest. I didn’t mean to make you feel alone—I just wanted to do things my way. Next time, I’ll ask you how you’d like me to help."* - This shows **teamwork** instead of **competition**. 4. **Small Gestures to Rebuild Trust** - **Next time she’s sick**, try: - Sitting with her for **even 20 minutes** while she rests. - Bringing her **her favorite tea or snacks** (not just medicine). - **Texting her** *"I’m thinking of you"* even if you’re busy. - **Physical touch** (holding her hand, rubbing her back) can mean more than words. 5. **Discuss "Caregiving Styles"** - Ask her: > *"What would make you feel most loved when you’re sick? Do you want me to be hands-on, or just nearby?"* - This **opens dialogue** instead of assuming you know what she needs. --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It Right or Wrong?** - **Neither.** It was a **mix of good intentions and miscommunication**. - **You weren’t an asshole**—you were **busy, stressed, and trying to balance responsibilities**. - **But you weren’t perfect either**—you didn’t **fully meet her emotional needs**, and your wife’s reaction was a **valid response** to feeling neglected. **This is a common issue in relationships**, especially with kids and work. The key is **not to repeat the same pattern**—next time, **ask her how she wants to be cared for**, and **show up in a way that feels meaningful to her**. --- ### **Score: 0.5/1 (Neither Fully Right Nor Wrong)** - **0.5** because your actions were **largely reasonable**, but the **emotional fallout** shows there was room for improvement in **communication and connection**. - **If you had asked her, *"How can I best support you right now?"*** before deciding, she might have felt **less abandoned**.
